idiom_name: plain struct + hand-written pack/unpack (or schema-generated nanopb/protobuf-c structs)
implementation_notes: C has no classes, so the DTO is a plain struct of fixed-width members and the assembler is an explicit encode/decode function pair over a byte buffer; ownership of every pointer member is the caller's job and must be documented next to the struct. Nothing of the classic bean-plus-serializer structure is absorbed - even field-by-field copying is written by hand. The hand-written form is justified only for a small, stable binary layout; otherwise let a schema generator (nanopb, protobuf-c) emit the struct and its encode/decode pair, which also keeps wire compatibility manageable.
pitfalls: sizeof(struct) is not the wire format: padding, alignment and endianness differ per compiler and architecture, so a struct must never be memcpy'd straight to the wire.
Pointer and flexible-array members have no implicit ownership: the encode/decode contract must say who allocates and frees nested data, and a failed decode must release whatever it already built.
Fixed char arrays truncate silently and may be unterminated; every variable-size field needs an explicit length.
